title: SEO and AI search for a browser game in plain Node.js: hreflang, JSON-LD, llms.txt and IndexNow without a framework
md:
*Disclosure: I build Towneers, a free multiplayer life sim in the browser. This is a write-up of how its site and blog are served. Everything below comes from the real code, simplified for reading.*

A browser game has an awkward SEO problem. The product is a canvas and a WebSocket, which a crawler sees as an empty page. The words that can rank, and that an AI assistant can quote, live somewhere else: a landing page, a game guide and a blog.

We decided not to bolt on a CMS or a static-site generator. The server already runs on plain Node.js, and the only runtime dependency is `ws`. So the blog is a single server module that renders HTML from markdown files. It also serves the machine-readable extras: feeds, sitemaps, `llms.txt` and a markdown copy of every post. This article walks through the decisions and the trade-offs.

## The shape of the system

Posts are files: `content/blog/<slug>/<lang>.md`, five languages (en, es, de, uk, ru). One module, `server/blog.js`, reads them, renders HTML on demand and caches the result in memory. The same engine also serves the `/game/...` guide pages, so there is only one place that knows how to emit `<head>`.

The header comment of the module lists what it promises: server-rendered text without scripts, a per-address and per-language in-memory cache, ETag and Last-Modified, gzip/brotli, canonical, hreflang with x-default, Open Graph, JSON-LD, RSS/Atom per language, a blog sitemap, `/llms.txt`, `/llms-full.txt` and a markdown version of each post at `/blog/<slug>.md`.

Why server rendering and not an SPA shell? A crawler, a link-preview bot and an LLM fetcher all share one trait: most of them do not run your JavaScript, or do not run it reliably. Plain HTML from a function is the most portable answer. The blog pages ship no framework code at all.

## Posts as files, with a tiny frontmatter

A post starts with a few lines of frontmatter. The parser in `shared/blog.js` is about twenty lines and handles only what we need: strings, `[a, b]` lists and booleans.

```js
export function parseFront(src) {
  const text = String(src ?? '').replace(/^﻿/, '').replace(/\r\n?/g, '\n');
  const m = /^---\n([\s\S]*?)\n---\n?/.exec(text);
  if (!m) return { meta: {}, body: text };
  const meta = {};
  for (const line of m[1].split('\n')) {
    const mm = /^([A-Za-z_][\w-]*)\s*:\s*(.*)$/.exec(line);
    if (!mm) continue;
    let v = mm[2].trim();
    if (/^\[.*\]$/.test(v)) v = v.slice(1, -1).split(',').map((x) => unq(x.trim())).filter(Boolean);
    else if (v === 'true' || v === 'false') v = v === 'true';
    else v = unq(v);
    meta[mm[1]] = v;
  }
  return { meta, body: text.slice(m[0].length) };
}
```

The fields are `title`, `description`, `summary`, `date`, `tags`, `cover` and `coverAlt`. A real post, trimmed:

```yaml
---
title: "Farming in Towneers: from your first seeds to a three-star harvest"
description: "A deep farming guide: plot prices, tools, all 9 crops, 5 seed tiers..."
date: 2026-11-27
tags: [guides, money]
cover: /landing/img/blog/farming-cover.webp
coverAlt: "A farm plot in North Farms at sunset..."
---
```

The decision here was to keep content in the repo, next to the code, and not in a database. Posts are reviewed and versioned like code. On the production server, edits made in the admin panel are written to a data directory that sits on top of the repo files. A store class re-scans the directories when the file signature changes, at most once every two seconds, and bumps a version counter. That counter is what invalidates the cache later.

## Custom blocks: FAQ, "try it" and tips

Markdown alone cannot express a FAQ that should become `FAQPage` markup, or a button that deep-links into the game. The renderer adds a small block syntax on top of markdown: `:::faq`, `:::try`, `:::tip`, plus `:::news` and `:::items`.

```md
:::try farms | ▶ Show me North Farms
...
:::

:::faq
### How much does a farm plot cost?
🪙2,700–5,400 right now. It depends on the size, and you can own up to 4 plots.
:::
```

The renderer collects every question and answer from a `:::faq` block into a list while it renders. That one list then feeds two outputs: the visible questions and answers, and the JSON-LD. Authors write the FAQ once and cannot make the markup disagree with the page. This "one source, several renderings" idea shows up again in the markdown copy and in `llms.txt`.

A caveat worth saying out loud: Google restricted FAQ rich results to a narrow set of sites some time ago, so you should not expect a FAQ snippet in the results. We still emit `FAQPage` because the structured question-and-answer pairs are cheap to produce and are exactly the shape that answer engines like to lift.

## The head: canonical, hreflang, Open Graph

One function, `page()`, builds the whole document. This is the part of the head that matters for multilingual SEO, reduced to the essentials:

```js
const xdef = alts.find((a) => a.lang === 'en');
return `<!doctype html>
<html lang="${lang}" dir="ltr">
<head>
  <title>${esc(title)}</title>
  <meta name="description" content="${esc(desc)}" />
  <meta name="robots" content="${robots}" />
  <link rel="canonical" href="${abs(canonical)}" />
  ${alts.map((a) => `<link rel="alternate" hreflang="${a.lang}" href="${abs(a.href)}" />`).join('\n  ')}
  ${xdef ? `<link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href="${abs(xdef.href)}" />` : ''}
  <meta property="og:type" content="${ogType}" />
  <meta property="og:locale" content="${ogLocale(lang)}" />
```

Three decisions are baked into this.

**hreflang lists only languages that exist.** A post has `alts` for the languages where a file is present, not for all five. Many sites generate alternates for every locale and point half of them at pages that do not exist or silently show English. We do not.

**x-default is English.** English lives at the unprefixed address (`/blog/...`), the other languages at `/blog/es/...`, `/blog/de/...` and so on. A request for `/blog/en/...` is redirected with a 301 to the unprefixed form so there is exactly one URL per page.

**Untranslated pages are noindexed.** If a post has no Spanish file, the Spanish address still works, because we do not want a dead end for a reader. It shows the English text with a "only in English for now" note. But the canonical points at the English URL and the robots meta becomes `noindex, follow`:

```js
const fallback = v.lang !== lang;
const canonical = fallback ? postPath('en', slug) : path;
// ...
robots: fallback || preview ? 'noindex, follow'
                            : 'index, follow, max-image-preview:large, max-snippet:-1',
```

There is no machine translation. A real translation is a separate file, and until it exists the page does not compete with itself in the index. Note `max-snippet:-1` and `max-image-preview:large` on real pages: we want long snippets, both for search and for AI answers.

Open Graph includes image width and height, `og:locale` and `og:locale:alternate` for the other languages, and `article:published_time`, `article:modified_time` and `article:tag` on posts. The cover image is a 1200×630 file. Link-preview bots (Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp and the rest) matter more for a social game than any search engine, and they read exactly these tags.

## JSON-LD: one graph per page type

Every post carries a `BlogPosting` plus a `BreadcrumbList`, and a `FAQPage` when the post has questions. This is the `BlogPosting` block, shortened:

```js
const postLd = {
  '@context': 'https://schema.org', '@type': 'BlogPosting', '@id': `${url}#post`,
  headline: v.title.slice(0, 110), description: v.description, url, inLanguage: v.lang,
  mainEntityOfPage: { '@type': 'WebPage', '@id': url },
  datePublished: `${v.date}T12:00:00Z`, dateModified: `${v.updated}T12:00:00Z`,
  author: { '@type': 'Organization', name: v.author || bt(v.lang, 'team'), url: `${origin}/` },
  publisher: { '@type': 'Organization', '@id': `${origin}/#org`, name: SITE, url: `${origin}/` },
  about: { '@type': 'VideoGame', name: SITE, url: `${origin}/` },
  wordCount: v.words, timeRequired: `PT${v.minutes}M`,
};
```

Notes on the choices:

- **Stable `@id`s.** `#post`, `#faq`, `#org`, `#game`. The organization and the game are referenced by id from many pages, so a consumer can merge them into one entity.
- **The game is a `VideoGame`.** The blog index describes it with `genre`, `gamePlatform`, `playMode: 'MultiPlayer'` and a free `Offer` (price 0). Every post says it is `about` that game, which ties the content to the product.
- **`HowTo` on guide pages.** The `/game/...` pages come from the same engine. A page can opt in with `howto: true` in its frontmatter, and the first numbered list becomes `HowToStep` items. The step name is the bold lead of each list item, so the visible text and the markup come from one list.
- **`wordCount` and `timeRequired`** are computed, not typed by hand.

The scenario document that describes this feature says a test checks that the JSON-LD parses and the fields are present. That is the only guard I would insist on: structured data fails silently, and a stray unescaped quote can make the whole block useless without any visible error.

## Numbers that cannot drift: `{{f:key}}` placeholders

Game guides are full of numbers: how many crops, what a plot costs, the market fee, the taxi fare. In a living game, the economy is tuned from an admin panel. A hand-typed number in an article is wrong the week after.

So guide pages use placeholders, and `server/sitefacts.js` computes the values from the same registries the game uses (items, recipes, catalog, the tuning table). A page says:

```md
Premises: rent from 🪙{{f:unit_rent_min}} a day (up to {{f:rent_biz_max}} rented at once)
or buy for 🪙{{f:unit_buy_min}}–{{f:unit_buy_max}}.
```

and the server fills it in at render time:

```js
const fillFacts = (md, lang) => md.replace(/\{\{f:([a-z0-9_]+)\}\}/g, (m, k) => {
  const v = facts()[k];
  return v == null ? '—' : typeof v === 'number' ? fmtNum(v, lang) : String(v);
});
```

Numbers are formatted in the reader's language. If the world has no data for a key, the page prints a dash instead of a wrong number. The facts are part of the cache version (`pages.ver | factsSig | store.ver`), so changing an economy value in the admin changes the rendered page, the ETag and `Last-Modified`, without a deploy.

The same text is what `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` expose, so a model that reads our site gets the current numbers and not a stale copy.

Trade-off: blog posts are different. They are dated snapshots, and there I allow typed numbers, because "prices on the day of writing" is the honest framing for a dated article. Placeholders are for the evergreen guide pages.

## Feeds and sitemaps

Per language, we serve RSS 2.0 at `/blog/feed.xml` (and `/blog/es/feed.xml` and so on) and Atom at `/blog/atom.xml`. Each page's head links to the feed of its own language.

There are two sitemaps, `/sitemap-blog.xml` and `/sitemap-game.xml`. Each URL entry lists its hreflang alternates, in the sitemap format, with the `xhtml:link` element:

```js
${u.alts.map((a) =>
  `<xhtml:link rel="alternate" hreflang="${a.lang}" href="${xml(origin + a.href)}" />`
).join('\n')}
${en ? `<xhtml:link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href="${xml(origin + en.href)}" />` : ''}
```

Putting hreflang in both the page head and the sitemap is redundant by design. The sitemap is easier to audit with a script, and the head is what a crawler sees when it lands on a single URL. If they ever disagree, you want to find that out in a test, not in Search Console.

## Speed and caching in a few dozen lines

The cache is a `Map` keyed by kind, language, path and origin. Each entry stores the rendered body, a version, an ETag and `Last-Modified`. If the store version has not changed, the same bytes come back. The cap is 600 entries, and the oldest one is dropped first.

```js
function cached(key, make, verOf = () => { store.scan(); return store.ver; }) {
  const ver = verOf();
  const hit = cache.get(key);
  if (hit && hit.ver === ver) return hit;
  const r = make();
  const body = Buffer.from(typeof r === 'string' ? r : r.html);
  const e = { ver, body, etag: etagOf(body),
              lastMod: new Date(Math.floor(lm / 1000) * 1000).toUTCString() };
  cache.set(key, e);
  if (cache.size > 600) cache.delete(cache.keys().next().value);
  return e;
}
```

The ETag is a truncated SHA-1 of the body. That is a content hash, so identical content gives an identical ETag across restarts. `send()` answers `If-None-Match` with a 304 and picks brotli or gzip from `Accept-Encoding`, compressing lazily and only once per entry (bodies under 1 KB are sent as-is):

```js
if (e.body.length > 1024 && /\bbr\b/.test(ae)) {
  e.br ||= brotliCompressSync(e.body, { params: { [Z.BROTLI_PARAM_QUALITY]: 6 } });
  body = e.br; head['Content-Encoding'] = 'br';
} else if (e.body.length > 1024 && /\bgzip\b/.test(ae)) {
  e.gz ||= gzipSync(e.body, { level: 7 }); body = e.gz; head['Content-Encoding'] = 'gzip';
}
```

Brotli at quality 6 is a compromise: much better than gzip on HTML, and cheap enough to do once per cached page. Quality 11 would be a bad idea on a request path. Responses carry `Cache-Control: public, max-age=..., stale-while-revalidate=86400` and a `Vary` header that depends on whether the address is language-negotiated.

The honest limit: this is a single-process, in-memory cache. It is right for one VPS and a few hundred pages. It would not survive being scaled to many instances without a shared layer or a CDN in front. For this site that is a fine trade.

## Language detection without hurting crawlers

The unprefixed English address has a split personality. For a human it should redirect to their language. For a crawler it must return the same English page every time, or the index becomes unstable.

The rule in `visitorLang()` runs in this order: the `?lang=` query parameter, then the cookie set by the game or the landing page (`tw_lang`), then a bot check, and only then `Accept-Language`. The bot check is a regex over the User-Agent that covers search crawlers, link-preview fetchers and AI agents:

```js
const BOT = /bot\b|bot\/|crawl|spider|slurp|facebookexternalhit|whatsapp|telegram|slack|discord
  |linkedin|preview|google|bing|yandex|applebot|gptbot|claude|anthropic|perplexity|ccbot
  |bytespider|amazonbot|duckassist|cohere|mistral|headless/i;

if (BOT.test(String(req.headers['user-agent'] || ''))) return DEFAULT_LANG;
```

(The real list is somewhat longer and I have shortened it here.) A bot gets English without a redirect. A redirect for a human is a 302 with `Vary: Accept-Language, Cookie` and `no-store`, so no cache ever pins a person to the wrong language. The redirect only happens if the page exists in that language, otherwise the visitor stays on the English page.

Is regex-matching user agents fragile? Yes. Any new bot that is not on the list will be treated like a person. But most crawlers send no `Accept-Language` header at all, so they fall through to English anyway. The regex mostly protects the case of a preview bot that does send one.

The landing page at `/` uses the same idea with a different URL scheme: `/?lang=es` for each language, hreflang for every dictionary, and `x-default` pointing at the bare origin. The server translates the Russian source of the page with the same dictionaries the game uses and caches the finished HTML per language. Link-share URLs carry `?lang=` of the person who shared, so a preview bot, which sends no `Accept-Language`, renders the card in the sharer's language.

## 404s that are really 404s

A not-found page returns status 404 with `Cache-Control: no-cache`, `noindex, follow`, and no hreflang alternates. It is a real page, with the latest three posts and a link to the blog and the home page, so a human who mistyped a URL has somewhere to go. The failure mode we avoid is the soft 404, a friendly page served with status 200 that a search engine will index as a duplicate.

Trailing slashes are redirected with a 301 to the clean path. Tag names are validated with a regex before any lookup, and a slug has to pass `validSlug`. These checks keep the number of crawlable URLs finite and boring.

## Markdown for machines: `/blog/<slug>.md`, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`

Each post exists in three renderings: HTML for people, JSON-LD for search engines, and markdown for language models. Markdown is available at the post address plus `.md`, and the HTML head advertises it:

```html
<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown" href="https://towneers.world/blog/farming-guide.md" />
```

The markdown copy is not the raw source file. A function `plainMarkdown()` produces it from the parsed post: the custom blocks are flattened, item icons are replaced with item names, the facts are filled in, and "try it" blocks become ordinary links with the deep-link URL. There are no scripts, no navigation and no layout.

`/llms.txt` follows the llmstxt.org layout. It describes the game, links to the key pages and posts as `.md` URLs, and lists feeds, sitemaps, and the per-language full-text files. `/llms-full.txt` contains the full text of every English guide page and post, and `/llms-full-es.txt`, `-de.txt`, `-uk.txt`, `-ru.txt` do the same per language.

I will not claim that `llms.txt` moves rankings. There is no public evidence that the major engines use it as a ranking signal, and the claims about it online are mostly speculation. My reason to keep it is cheaper: it is one cached function over data we already have, and some agents and developer tools do fetch it. The `.md` endpoints cost almost nothing and give any fetcher a clean copy to quote.

## robots.txt: the AI crawler decision

The file is static (`client/robots.txt`) and the decision is written in a comment at the top: AI crawlers and AI search assistants are welcome on the site and the blog. The list names GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, Claude-User, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, Perplexity-User, Google-Extended, Applebot-Extended, CCBot, Meta-ExternalAgent, Bytespider, Amazonbot, DuckAssistBot, cohere-ai and MistralAI-User. Every one gets the same rules as everybody else:

```
User-agent: *
Allow: /
Allow: /blog/
Allow: /game/
Allow: /llms.txt
Allow: /llms-full.txt
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /api/
Disallow: /pay/
Disallow: /play

Sitemap: https://towneers.world/sitemap-blog.xml
Sitemap: https://towneers.world/sitemap-game.xml
```

Two things deserve a note. First, repeating the rules for each named agent is required in practice: a crawler that finds a group for its own name ignores the `*` group, so an explicit group with only `Allow` lines would otherwise hide the `Disallow` lines. We repeat them. Second, `/play`, the game itself, is disallowed for everyone. There is nothing to index in a canvas, and crawlers should not create sessions.

This is a business decision and not a technical one. For a free game that lives on word of mouth, being recommended by an assistant is distribution, so we opted in. If your content is your product, you may decide the opposite. The point is to make the decision explicit and write the reasoning in the file, so that reversing it later means deleting a few lines.

## IndexNow: telling search engines instead of waiting

Sitemaps are polled, so a new post can wait days to be noticed. IndexNow is a push protocol supported by Bing, Yandex, Seznam and others, and Bing's index is one of the feeds behind several AI search products. `server/indexnow.js` is 75 lines with no dependencies.

On production only, it generates a 32-hex key once and stores it in the data directory. It serves the key as `/<key>.txt`, which is how the protocol verifies that you own the host. Then, on a timer, it reads our own sitemaps (the same functions that serve them) and compares each `lastmod` with a small JSON file of what it already sent:

```js
export function changedUrls(entries, sent) {
  return entries.filter((e) => e.loc.startsWith(ORIGIN + '/') && sent[e.loc] !== e.lastmod);
}
// ...
const r = await fetchFn(API, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json; charset=utf-8' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ host: HOST, key, keyLocation: `${ORIGIN}/${key}.txt`,
                         urlList: list.map((e) => e.loc) }),
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000),
});
if (r.status !== 200 && r.status !== 202) return 0;   // retry on the next tick
```

It first runs two minutes after start, then every 30 minutes, and sends at most 10,000 URLs per call. Only `200` and `202` count as success, and only then are the URLs recorded as sent, so a failed call is retried by the next tick. The sitemap is the single source of truth for what changed: no hooks in the admin or the deploy script, no separate list to maintain. An `INDEXNOW=off` environment switch disables it. The timers are `unref()`'d so they never keep the process alive.

Google does not support IndexNow, so for Google the sitemaps remain the way in.

## From article to game: deep links

A blog that cannot send a reader into the product is just a blog. The `:::try` block renders a call-to-action that opens the game at a specific place, `/play?go=<place>`, from a fixed whitelist (`funfair`, `fame`, `square`, `market`, `carshop`, `realty`, `cottages`, `farms`, `beach`, `park`, `football`). The client reads the parameter and shows the player the way to that place. An unknown value falls back to a plain `start=new` link.

The server appends UTM parameters, with the post slug as the campaign:

```js
const playUrl = (campaign) => (go) =>
  `/play?${GO_PLACES.includes(go) ? `go=${go}&` : 'start=new&'}` +
  `utm_source=blog&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=${encodeURIComponent(campaign)}`;
```

So every post is measurable as a channel, and the markdown copy contains the same link. Since `/play` is disallowed in robots.txt, these links are for people, not for crawlers to follow.

## What I would do differently

- **Test the head, not just the body.** Our scenario document says a test verifies that JSON-LD parses and the fields exist. I would add a check that every hreflang target returns 200 and links back, because broken return links make hreflang get ignored.
- **Do not trust a rich result to appear.** Structured data is eligibility, not a promise.
- **Keep the cache honest.** A version counter is simpler than invalidation by key, but it throws away everything when one post changes. At our size that costs milliseconds. At ten thousand pages it would not.
- **Measure AI referrals directly.** UTM tags work only when the assistant keeps them. Server logs by user agent are the other half of the picture.

## Checklist

1. Server-render the text. No client JS is needed to read a page.
2. One canonical URL per page. Redirect `/en/`-style duplicates and trailing slashes with 301.
3. hreflang only for languages that really exist, plus `x-default`. Put it in the head and in the sitemap.
4. Untranslated fallback pages: show something useful, canonical to the original, `noindex, follow`.
5. Real 404 status, `noindex`, no alternates.
6. Open Graph with image size, `og:locale` and its alternates; a 1200×630 cover.
7. JSON-LD with stable `@id`s: `BlogPosting`, `BreadcrumbList`, `FAQPage`, `HowTo`, and a `VideoGame` for the product.
8. Generate FAQ markup from the same list that renders the visible FAQ.
9. Put changing numbers behind placeholders computed from live data.
10. ETag from a content hash, `Last-Modified`, `Cache-Control` with `stale-while-revalidate`, brotli with gzip as the fallback.
11. Never redirect bots by language. Check the User-Agent before `Accept-Language`.
12. RSS and Atom per language, linked from the head.
13. Sitemaps with hreflang alternates; list them in robots.txt.
14. A markdown copy of each page, linked with `rel="alternate" type="text/markdown"`, and an `llms.txt` over it.
15. Decide your AI crawler policy on purpose, repeat the disallow rules in every named group, and write the reasoning in the file.
16. Push changes with IndexNow from your own sitemap, and record what was sent.
17. Deep-link from content into the product with UTM tags on every link.

None of this needs a framework. It needs one module that treats every page as data and renders it several ways.

If you want to see what all of this serves, the game is free and runs in any browser. [towneers.world](https://towneers.world/r/hashnode?utm_campaign=seo-node&utm_content=article)
